book_title: Chapter 3: Routes to Market, Cocoa Hedging & Every Dollar Through the P&L
question: How does Mondelēz move snacks from cocoa farms and bakeries to millions of shelves, and where does every $100 of revenue go?

epigraph.quote: Brands win the mind, but route-to-market wins the impulse; the difference between a warehouse drop and a kirana cooler is the difference between a commodity and a habit.
epigraph.author: Supply Chain & Route-to-Market Field Note

web_blocks.html: Mondelēz's distribution model is a tale of two worlds. In emerging markets—spanning India, Brazil, Mexico, China, and Southeast Asia—Mondelēz runs one of the deepest traditional-trade networks in global staples. In India alone, its products reach over 5 million retail outlets [12, 22]. Management also added approximately 130,000 new outlets year-to-date through Q3 2026 [12, 22]. In Brazil, Mondelēz surpassed 1 million direct and indirect stores in 2026 [12]. COO Luca Zaramella noted on the Q3 2026 call that roughly 25% additional numeric distribution runway remains across India, China, and Brazil [12]. Mondelēz pairs that store reach with larger Visi coolers and higher SKU counts per outlet [12]. This last-mile network—combining company sales reps, sub-distributors, and B2B digital ordering—forms a strong barrier against regional rivals [22, 26].

In North America, by contrast, Mondelēz relies primarily on a warehouse-delivered model to retailer central distribution centers [22]. It does not operate a universal Direct Store Delivery (DSD) fleet [22]. Historically, Nabisco ran a DSD network before transitioning to warehouse delivery to cut fixed logistics costs and lift operating margins into the ~18%–23% range [21, 22]. Warehouse delivery is highly capital-efficient and supports >95% ACV in center-store cookie and cracker aisles [22]. However, Mondelēz lacks the daily driver-merchandiser presence that PepsiCo's Frito-Lay commands at front-end checkout impulse racks and convenience-store end-caps [22]. To offset that gap, Mondelēz is investing in North American supply-chain modernization and a $1.2 billion multi-year global ERP transformation [12, 27]. The ERP rollout finished in North America and Latin America in 2026 and extends globally through 2028 to sharpen demand forecasting, promotional ROI, and inventory turns [12, 27].

On the input-cost side, four primary raw materials govern Mondelēz's unit economics: cocoa (beans, butter, and liquor), wheat flour, sugar, and dairy, plus packaging and freight [16, 22]. Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana supply ~60% of global cocoa, exposing the crop to severe weather and disease cycles [16, 22]. Mondelēz manages that volatility with a rolling 12-to-18-month hedging book using exchange-traded futures, options, and physical forward contracts [16, 22]. At the same time, it diversifies physical sourcing toward Latin America and Asia through its Cocoa Life program [16, 22]. When cocoa spiked above $10,000/ton in 2024, hedges delayed—but could not prevent—a 580 bps drop in Adjusted Gross Margin in FY2025 (from 37.8% to 32.0%) and a 1,070 bps drop in GAAP Gross Margin (to 28.4%) [10, 15, 16]. Conversely, a ~500,000-ton global cocoa surplus in 2025/2026 pushed spot prices below $3,000/ton [12, 15, 17]. Lower-cost inventory began flowing into the P&L in Q3 2026, lifting Adjusted Gross Margin +380 bps YoY to 34.2%, with full normalization expected in 2027 [12, 15, 17].

Beyond routing and hedging, two operational programs shape Mondelēz's 2025–2028 cost structure: regulatory cocoa traceability and ERP modernization. Europe absorbs 58% of global cocoa production [15]. Under the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), companies must prove farm-level geolocation traceability or face penalties of at least 4% of annual EU turnover [15]. Mondelēz's decade-long investment in Cocoa Life gives it a compliance and data-mapping edge over smaller regional confectioners that rely on spot intermediaries [22, 24]. Simultaneously, the $1.2 billion ERP System Implementation program (with $1.2 billion in board-approved funding, largely expensed in SG&A through 2028) completed its initial phase in North America and Latin America in 2026 [12, 27]. That system replaces fragmented legacy SAP instances with a unified global supply-chain backbone [12, 27].

Working-capital discipline is an equally important pillar of Mondelēz's unit economics. At December 31, 2025, Mondelēz held $3,903 million in trade receivables (~37 days sales outstanding) and $4,419 million in inventories (~58 days, elevated by higher-cost cocoa) [10]. Against those assets, it carried $10,139 million in accounts payable (~134 days payable outstanding) [10]. That negative cash-conversion cycle means suppliers effectively finance a substantial share of Mondelēz's finished-goods inventory and retail receivables [10]. Even in FY2025, when higher-cost cocoa inflated inventory carrying values by $592 million year-over-year, disciplined receivables collection (+$433M cash inflow) kept operating cash flow at $4,514 million [10].

web_blocks.caption: Audited FY2025 GAAP Unit Economics Waterfall ($ Millions, per FY2025 Form 10-K / Earnings Release)
web_blocks.takeaway: Employee costs are not separately broken out in GAAP 10-K disclosures and are embedded within COGS ($27,602M, including manufacturing depreciation) and SG&A ($7,173M, combined with $85M impairments less $13M divestiture gain = $7,245M other_opex). Separately reported intangible amortization is $142M (total consolidated D&A on the Cash Flow Statement is $1,358M). GAAP Operating Income of $3,548M (9.2% margin) was depressed by $1,379M of unrealized derivative mark-to-market losses; stripping out non-cash MTM and working capital swings, CFO reached $4,514M and Free Cash Flow totaled $3,235M after $1,279M Capex (3.3% of revenue).

web_blocks.title: Unit Economics Forensic Check: Why FCF Exceeded GAAP Net Earnings by 31% in FY2025
paragraphs: In FY2025, Mondelēz converted $38,537 million of revenue into $2,466 million of GAAP net earnings (6.4% net margin) [10]. Yet it generated $4,514 million in operating cash flow and $3,235 million in Free Cash Flow (8.4% FCF margin, or 131% of GAAP net earnings) [10].

The bridge is straightforward: GAAP net earnings absorbed $1,379 million in non-cash unrealized derivative losses plus $1,358 million in D&A [10]. Meanwhile, disciplined Capex ($1,279 million, or 3.3% of sales) preserved strong cash generation [10].

web_blocks.html: 9M 2026 Derivative MTM & Working-Capital Friction: In the first nine months of 2026, Mondelēz recorded a $1,091 million unrealized gain on derivative contracts—reversing the $1,161 million unrealized loss in 9M 2025 [29]. That non-cash swing lifted 9M 2026 GAAP gross margin to 36.4% (39.4% in Q3 2026) versus 32.9% Adjusted Gross Margin (34.2% in Q3 2026) [12, 29]. On a cash basis, however, derivative settlements generated a $245 million net cash outflow in 9M 2026 ($210 million proceeds vs. $455 million payments), while trade receivables expanded by $1,016 million from December 31, 2025 to $4,919 million at September 30, 2026 (a $1,212 million operating cash-flow drag) [29].

book_paragraphs: To understand how Mondelēz makes money, you have to look at two very different distribution engines operating under the same corporate roof. In emerging markets—India, Brazil, Mexico, China—Mondelēz plays a high-touch, traditional-trade game. In India alone, its chocolates and biscuits sit inside more than 5 million retail outlets, and management added another 130,000 stores in the first nine months of 2026. In Brazil, the company just crossed 1 million stores. When COO Luca Zaramella tells analysts they still have 25% numeric distribution runway left in India, China, and Brazil, he is describing a multi-year physical land grab where every new Visi cooler placed on a shopkeeper's counter locks out smaller competitors.

Now contrast that with North America. Here, Mondelēz largely uses a warehouse-delivered model rather than a Direct Store Delivery fleet. Instead of driving thousands of route trucks straight to convenience stores every morning like Frito-Lay does, Mondelēz ships full pallets from regional bakeries to retailer distribution centers. That warehouse model is remarkably efficient—it is a big reason North America earns 18% to 23% operating margins—but it comes with a real trade-off. Mondelēz dominates the center-store cookie and cracker aisle with over 95% distribution, yet it has less control over front-end checkout impulse racks than DSD-backed rivals.

Inside the factories, unit economics revolve around cocoa, wheat, sugar, dairy, packaging, and freight. Cocoa is the wildcard. Because roughly 60% of the world's cocoa comes from Ivory Coast and Ghana, a bad harvest can double or triple raw-material costs in months. Mondelēz hedges 12 to 18 months forward using futures and forward contracts. That smooths out normal volatility, but when cocoa surged over 365% into 2024, the hedges simply delayed the blow until 2025.

Let's walk every $100 of Mondelēz's audited 2025 revenue of $38.54 billion straight down the income statement so you can see the damage—and the cash-flow reality—with your own eyes. Out of every $100 in sales, cost of goods sold consumed $71.60 in 2025, leaving $28.40 in GAAP gross profit, down nearly 11 percentage points from $39.10 in 2024. Why? Both higher physical cocoa costs and $1.38 billion in non-cash mark-to-market derivative losses hit cost of sales. Next, selling, general, and administrative expenses—including advertising, sales teams, and corporate overhead—took $18.60, plus another $0.60 for intangible amortization and restructuring, leaving just $9.20 in GAAP operating profit.

After paying $0.73 in net interest, absorbing $0.05 in net pension and equity-method items, and paying $2.03 in income taxes, Mondelēz kept $6.40 in GAAP net earnings per $100 of revenue, or $2.47 billion total. If you stopped there, you might think the business was struggling. But look at the cash flow statement: adding back $3.52 in depreciation and amortization and $3.58 in non-cash derivative losses, less working capital movements, produced $11.71 in operating cash flow per $100 of sales ($4.51 billion). Subtracting $3.32 in capital expenditures ($1.28 billion, or just 3.3% of revenue) left $8.39 in pure Free Cash Flow per $100 of sales—$3.24 billion in total. That is why a forensic cash-flow check matters so much: even in its worst commodity-margin year in a decade, Mondelēz's free cash flow exceeded its GAAP net income by more than 30%.

There are two other operational realities in the supply chain that you should keep on your radar: regulatory traceability in Europe and the $1.2 billion global ERP overhaul. Europe accounts for nearly half of global chocolate sales, and the European Union Deforestation Regulation now requires companies to prove their cocoa did not come from deforested land—with fines reaching 4% of annual turnover for non-compliance. Because Mondelēz spent the past decade building its Cocoa Life sourcing network directly with farming cooperatives, it has a real compliance head start over smaller competitors that buy anonymous beans on the spot market.

At the same time, Mondelēz is halfway through a $1.2 billion multi-year ERP transformation to unify its supply-chain and financial systems worldwide. The first phase went live in North America and Latin America in 2026, with the remaining regions rolling out through 2028. That spending shows up as an operating expense drag today, which is why management strips it out of adjusted earnings, but once complete it should tighten inventory turns, sharpen promotional analytics, and reduce working-capital friction across 80 countries.

Before we leave the unit-economics chapter, take a quick look at the working-capital engine hiding on Mondelēz's balance sheet. At the end of 2025, Mondelēz carried $3.90 billion in customer receivables and $4.42 billion in raw-material and finished-goods inventory. Against that $8.32 billion in working assets, it owed suppliers $10.14 billion in accounts payable. In plain English, Mondelēz collects cash from supermarkets and distributors far faster than it pays its packaging, flour, and cocoa vendors.

That negative working-capital cycle is why Mondelēz runs comfortably with a 0.62x current ratio without any operational stress. Even when sky-high cocoa prices inflated the dollar value of its chocolate inventory by nearly $600 million in 2025, tight receivables collection helped keep operating cash flow above $4.5 billion. When cocoa prices fall, that working-capital effect reverses into an extra cash tailwind as lower-cost beans replace expensive inventory.

Let's also examine what happens inside Mondelēz's manufacturing plants when cocoa prices swing 300% in two years. Chocolate is not just cocoa butter and cocoa liquor; it is a delicate formulation balancing cocoa mass, milk solids, sugar, and emulsifiers. When cocoa costs soared in 2024 and 2025, Mondelēz did not compromise the signature taste profile of Cadbury Dairy Milk or Milka—a mistake that has permanently damaged food brands in past inflation cycles. Instead, its supply-chain engineers focused on conversion productivity, factory automation, and waste reduction, while its commercial teams used Revenue Growth Management to adjust pack weights and promotional frequency.

On the Q3 2026 call, CFO Amit Banati specifically credited those supply-chain conversion and procurement productivity savings—alongside lower cocoa costs and volume operating leverage—for driving the 380-basis-point rebound in Adjusted Gross Margin to 34.2%. That tells us the factories are getting leaner even as the commodity cycle turns favorable.

The first nine months of 2026 proved that derivative mark-to-market accounting cuts both ways. As spot cocoa retreated, Mondelēz booked a $1,091 million unrealized derivative gain in 9M 2026—reversing the $1,161 million unrealized loss from 9M 2025—which flattered Q3 2026 GAAP gross margin to 39.4% compared with 34.2% on an adjusted basis. Beneath the surface, actual cash derivative settlements still resulted in a $245 million net cash outflow, and trade receivables swelled by $1,016 million to $4.92 billion at September 30, 2026, creating a $1.21 billion working-capital drag ahead of the fourth-quarter seasonal collection wave.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: The Double-Edged Sword of 18-Month Hedging
book_callouts.text: Investors often assume hedging eliminates commodity risk. In reality, rolling 12-to-18-month hedges only buy time to adjust retail prices and pack sizes. When spot cocoa crashes as it did in 2026, those same hedges delay the margin rebound—which is why patient analysts track physical crop surpluses and hedge roll-offs rather than reacting to a single quarter's GAAP gross margin.
